en: Thus have I heard: the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta, Discourse on the Fool and the Wise, from the Majjhima Nikāya, number 129.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of a fool, signs of a fool, and grounds for being called a fool.”
Which three?
Here, monks, a fool is one who thinks ill-thought thoughts, speaks ill-spoken speech, and performs ill-done deeds.
If, monks, this fool were not one who thinks ill-thought thoughts, speaks ill-spoken speech, and performs ill-done deeds, how would the wise know him as such?
‘This worthy man is a fool, an untrue person’?
It is because, monks, a fool thinks evil thoughts, speaks evil words, and performs evil deeds, that the wise know him:
‘This worthy man is a fool, an untrue person.’
Indeed, monks, that fool experiences three kinds of suffering and mental distress right here and now in this very life.
If, monks, that fool is sitting in an assembly, or sitting on a street, or sitting at a crossroads,
and people there engage in conversation that is relevant and appropriate to the occasion.
“Bhikkhus, if a fool is one who destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants that cause negligence,
then, bhikkhus, it occurs to that fool:
‘Whatever people say regarding such a person, whatever they discuss as appropriate for him— ’”
‘Those qualities truly exist in me, and I am seen to possess those qualities.
Monks, this is the first way in which a fool experiences suffering and mental distress even in this very life.
Furthermore, monks, a fool sees kings who, having seized a thief or a wrongdoer, subject them to various forms of punishment.
Even when they are being beaten with whips, beaten with canes, beaten with split bamboo,
or when their hands are cut off, their feet are cut off, both hands and feet are cut off, their ears are cut off, their noses are cut off, both ears and noses are cut off,
or when they are made to undergo the "spit-ox" torture, the "conch-shell-shaven" torture, or the "Rāhu’s mouth" torture.
Whether they were making garlands of fire, holding torches in their hands, forming circles of reeds, wearing garments of bark, acting like antelopes,
using hooks as ornaments, performing the "kahāpaṇa" rite, undergoing the "khārāpatacchika" (scouring with caustic lye),
performing the "palighaparivattika" (turning on a crossbar), performing the "palālapīṭhaka" (lying on a bed of straw), or being doused with boiling oil.
They have him fed to dogs, impaled alive on stakes, or have his head cut off with a sword.
In that situation, monks, it occurs to the fool:
"It is for the sake of such evil deeds that kings, having seized a thief who has committed a crime, inflict various forms of punishment."
They flog me with whips... up to ... they even decapitate me with swords;
those things indeed exist in me, and I am seen to possess those things.
Even if kings were to know of me, they would seize me and subject me to various forms of torture.
"They might flog him with whips... [and so on] ...they might impale him alive on a stake, or they might cut off his head with a sword.
Monks, this too is the second kind of suffering and mental distress that a fool experiences here and now in this very life.
Furthermore, monks, when a fool has mounted a chair or a bed, or is on the ground—

When he is lying down, those evil deeds he previously committed—misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind—hang over him at that time, hang down upon him, and hang all around him.

Just as, monks, the shadows of great mountain peaks in the evening time hang over the earth, hang down upon it, and hang all around it; so too, when he is lying down, those evil deeds... hang all around him.
In the same way, monks, when a fool has ascended onto a chair, or onto a bed, or is lying on the ground,
those evil deeds he previously committed— misconduct by body, misconduct by speech,
and misconduct by mind— hang upon him at that time, hang down upon him, and dangle over him.
In this regard, monks, it occurs to the fool thus:
"Alas, I have not done what is beautiful, I have not done what is wholesome, I have not done what provides a refuge from fear;
I have done evil, I have done cruel deeds, I have done sinful acts."

‘To whatever destination those who have not done what is good, who have not done what is wholesome, who have not provided a refuge for themselves in times of fear, who have committed evil, who have been cruel, and who have committed crimes go after death— to that same destination I shall go,’ he grieves,
he is exhausted, he laments, he beats his breast and weeps, and he falls into delusion. This too, monks,
is the third kind of suffering and mental distress that a fool experiences here and now in this very life.

“Monks, that fool, having practiced misconduct by body, having practiced misconduct by speech, and having practiced misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
Monks, one speaking rightly would say of that which is exclusively undesirable, exclusively unlovely, and exclusively disagreeable: ‘Hell indeed is what one should speak of as such.’”
“‘Entirely undesirable, entirely unlovely, entirely disagreeable.
Monks, it is not easy to find even a simile for how painful the hells are.
When this was said, a certain monk addressed the Blessed One in this way:
“But is it possible, venerable sir, to give a simile?
“It is possible, bhikkhus,” the Blessed One said.
“Suppose, bhikkhu, they were to seize a thief caught in the act of wrongdoing and present him to the king, saying:”
‘Sire, this is indeed a thief, a perpetrator of violence; inflict upon him whatever punishment you wish.
Then the king might say to them:
‘Go, sirs, in the morning, strike this man with a hundred spears.’”
Suppose they were to strike him with a hundred spears in the morning.
Then, at midday, the king might ask:
"Hey, what has become of that man?"
‘In that very same way, Your Majesty, he is still alive.
Then the king would say to him:
‘Go, sirs, at the time of midday, strike that man with a hundred spears.’
Suppose they were to strike him with a hundred spears at midday.
Then, in the evening, the king might ask:
"Ho there! What is that man like?"
‘In the same way, Your Majesty, he is still alive.
Then the king would say to him:
‘Go, sirs, and at the evening hour strike that man with a hundred spears.’”
Suppose they were to strike him with a hundred spears in the evening.
What do you think, monks,
would that man, being struck by those three hundred spears, experience pain and distress on that account?”
“Venerable sir, if that man were struck by even a single spear, he would experience pain and grief on that account; what need is there to speak of three hundred spears?
Then the Blessed One took up a small stone about the size of his hand and addressed the bhikkhus:
“What do you think, bhikkhus?”
“Which, indeed, is greater: this small stone, the size of my hand, that I have taken up, or Himavā, the king of mountains?

“Venerable sir, the small stone, the size of the Blessed One’s hand, that has been taken up by the Blessed One is insignificant; compared to Himavā, the king of mountains, it does not even admit of a numerical comparison, it does not admit of a fractional comparison, it does not even admit of a resemblance.
“In the same way, bhikkhus, as for the suffering that would arise from that man being struck with three hundred spears...”
He experiences mental distress that, compared to the suffering of hell,
does not even approach a fraction of it, nor a part of it,
nor can it be compared to it at all. Then, monks, the wardens of hell inflict upon him a judicial torture called the "fivefold bondage."
They drive a red-hot iron stake through one hand; they drive a red-hot iron stake through the other hand;
they drive a red-hot iron stake through one foot; they drive a red-hot iron stake through the other foot; they drive a red-hot iron stake through the middle of the chest.
There he experiences painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations, yet he does not die as long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell, having laid him down, pare him with axes.
There he experiences pain that is sharp... [as before] ...and it comes to an end.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell, seizing him by his feet and holding him upside down, pare him with adzes.
There, monks, he experiences painful, sharp... [as before] ... that comes to an end.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell yoke him to a chariot and drive him back and forth over a ground that is burning, blazing, and glowing.
There, monks, he experiences painful, sharp... [as before] ... that comes to an end.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell make him climb up and down a great mountain of glowing coals—blazing, fiercely burning, and aflame.
There he experiences feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter; yet he does not die so long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell seize him by his feet and head, and cast him into a heated iron cauldron—blazing, fiercely burning, and aflame.
There he is cooked in a mass of foam.
While being cooked there in that mass of foam, he goes up at one time, down at another, and across at another.
There he experiences painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations; yet he does not die as long as that evil karma has not been exhausted.
Then, monks, the wardens of hell cast him into the Great Hell.
Now, monks, that Great Hell has four corners and four gates.
Divided and measured out into portions,
it is surrounded by an iron wall and closed in with iron.
For him, the ground is made of iron,
blazing and filled with heat for a hundred yojanas all around.
It remains pervading them at all times.
Monks, I could speak on the matter of hell in many ways;
indeed, monks, it is not easy to reach the end of describing how painful the hells are.
“Bhikkhus, there are animals that subsist on grass.
They chew up grass, whether it is fresh or dry, by licking it with their teeth.
And what, bhikkhus, are those animals that subsist on grass?”
Elephants, horses, oxen, donkeys, goats, deer, or whatever other animals there may be that subsist on grass— monks,
that fool who was formerly a lover of flavors here and has performed evil deeds here, upon the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn into the company of those beings who subsist on grass.
Monks, there are also animals that subsist on dung.
Having smelled the stench of excrement from afar, they run toward it, thinking, “We shall eat here! We shall eat here!
Just as brahmins run toward the scent of a sacrificial offering:
‘We shall eat here, we shall eat here’—
even so, monks, there are animals that feed on dung which,
having smelled the scent of dung from afar, run toward it:
‘We shall eat here, we shall eat here.
And what, monks, are the animals that live on dung?
Chickens, pigs, dogs, jackals, and whatever other animals there are that live on dung.

“Monks, that fool who was formerly a lover of flavors here, having performed evil deeds here, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn into the company of those beings who feed on excrement.
There are, monks, animals born in darkness, living in darkness, and dying in darkness.
And what, monks, are those animals born in darkness, living in darkness, and dying in darkness?”
Worms, insects, and ants, or whatever other creatures there may be belonging to the animal realm that are born in darkness, live in darkness, and die in darkness. A fool, monks,
who was formerly a glutton for flavors here and having performed evil deeds here,
at the breaking up of the body, after death, is reborn into the company of those beings who are born in darkness.
In darkness they are born; in darkness they die.
There are, monks, animals belonging to the animal realm that are born in water, live in water, and die in water.
And what, monks, are those animals belonging to the animal realm that are born in water, live in water, and die in water?
Fish, turtles, crocodiles, or whatever other beings there may be belonging to the animal realm that are born in water, live in water, and die in water. Monks, that fool—
who was previously a relisher of flavors here and performed evil deeds here—
upon the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn into the company of those beings who are born in water.
In water they are born, in water they grow, and in water they die.
There are, bhikkhus, animals that are born in filth, grow in filth, and die in filth.
And what, bhikkhus, are those animals that are born in filth, grow in filth, and die in filth?
Those beings, monks, who are born in rotten fish, or grow old in rotten fish, or die in rotten fish, or in putrid corpses … [and so on] … or in putrid sour gruel,
or in cesspools … [and so on] … [are reborn there].
or among dung beetles; or whatever other animals there may be that are born in filth, live in filth, and die in filth.

That fool, monks, having been a lover of flavors here in the past and having performed evil deeds here, at the breaking up of the body, after death, is reborn into the company of those beings who are born in filth.
In impurity they are born, and in impurity they die.
Monks, I could speak on the subject of animal rebirth in many ways;
indeed, monks, it is not easy to reach the end of this matter through mere description, for so painful is the animal realm.
"Suppose, monks, a man were to throw a yoke with a single hole into the great ocean.
An easterly wind would drive it westward; a westerly wind would drive it eastward; a northerly wind would drive it southward; and a southerly wind would drive it northward.
There, a blind turtle, rising once every hundred years, would surface."
“What do you think, bhikkhus,
would that blind turtle put its neck into that yoke with a single hole in it?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“But if, venerable sir, after the passing of a long period of time, at some point or other,” [he asked].

“More quickly, monks, would that blind turtle insert its neck into that single-holed yoke; yet, monks, I say that human status is even more difficult to obtain for a fool who has once fallen into the lower realms. And why is that?
"Monks, here there is no practice of the Dhamma, no practice of rectitude, no performance of wholesome deeds, and no performance of meritorious deeds.
Here, monks, there prevails mutual devouring—the devouring of the weak.
If, monks, that fool should at some time or other, after the lapse of a long period, attain human birth, he will be born into low families—"
Or he is reborn into a family of outcasts, or a family of hunters, or a family of bamboo-workers, or a family of cartwrights, or a family of refuse-removers—
a family that is poor, lacking food and drink, with a difficult livelihood, where even basic sustenance and clothing are obtained only with great difficulty.
Furthermore, he is ugly, unsightly, deformed, afflicted by many diseases— perhaps one-eyed, or with a withered arm, or hunchbacked, or paralyzed on one side.
Or he does not obtain food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, or lighting.
He engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.

Having engaged in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
“Just as, monks, a gambler might lose his son at the very first throw of the dice, or lose his wife, or lose all his property, and even incur further bondage;

yet, monks, that loss at the first throw of the dice—whereby he loses his son, his wife, all his property, and incurs further bondage—is a mere trifle. Why is that? Because, monks, there is another throw of the dice that is far more ruinous than that.”
But even greater than that is this misfortune: that a fool, having practiced misconduct by body,
having practiced misconduct by speech, and having practiced misconduct by mind, after the breakup of the body, after death,
reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
"This, monks, is the entire, complete domain of the fool.
"Monks, there are these three characteristics of a wise person, marks of a wise person, and attributes of a wise person.
What are the three?"
In this case, monks, a wise person is one who thinks well-thought thoughts, speaks well-spoken words, and performs well-done deeds.
For if, monks, that wise person were not one who thinks well-thought thoughts, speaks well-spoken words, and performs well-done deeds, how would the wise know him as:
"This worthy man is a wise person"?
But because, monks, a wise person is one who thinks well-thought thoughts, speaks well-spoken words, and performs well-done deeds, therefore the wise recognize him, saying:
"This worthy person is wise.
That wise person, monks, experiences three kinds of happiness and joy even here and now.
If, monks, a wise person is sitting in an assembly, or sitting on a street, or sitting at a crossroads,
and people there are discussing matters that are relevant and appropriate;
if, monks, that wise person abstains from the destruction of life and abstains from taking what is not given...
He abstains from sexual misconduct, he abstains from false speech, and he abstains from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.
In this regard, monks, the wise person thinks thus:
‘Whatever talk people discuss that is relevant and appropriate to that situation;’
‘Those qualities truly exist in me, and I am seen to possess those qualities.
Monks, this is the first way a wise person experiences happiness and joy in this very life.
Furthermore, monks, a wise person sees kings who, having seized a thief or a wrongdoer, inflict various forms of punishment upon them—
Even when they are being beaten with whips, beaten with canes, beaten with split bamboo;
when their hands are cut off, their feet are cut off, both hands and feet are cut off; when their ears are cut off, their noses are cut off, both ears and noses are cut off;
when they are made to undergo the "spit-ox" torture, the "conch-shell-head" torture, or the "Rāhu’s mouth" torture.
Whether they make him wear a garland of fire, or carry a torch in his hand, or make him turn a *eraka*-grass whorl,
or dress him in bark garments, or make him wear a deer-skin, or make him carry a fish-hook, or make him carry a coin,
or have him scraped with salt and wood-shavings, or make him roll under a crossbar, or make him sit on a straw mat, or pour boiling oil over him—
They have him fed to dogs, impaled alive on stakes, or have his head cut off with a sword.
In this regard, monks, a wise person thinks:
"It is for the sake of such evil deeds that kings, having seized a thief who has committed a crime, subject him to various forms of punishment."
They cause them to be punished; they beat them with whips, they beat them with canes, they beat them with split rods;
they cut off their hands, they cut off their feet, they cut off both hands and feet; they cut off their ears, they cut off their noses, they cut off both ears and noses;
they subject them to the *bilaṅgathālika* torture, they subject them to the *saṅkhamuṇḍika* torture.
They make [the victim] resemble Rāhu’s mouth; they make him wear a garland of fire; they make him carry a torch in his hand;
they make him wear a wreath of *eraka* grass; they make him wear a garment of bark; they make him wear a deerskin; they make him carry a fishhook;
they make him carry a *kahāpaṇa* coin; they make him undergo the scourging with salt; they make him turn over a crossbar.
‘They even make a seat of straw for me, they sprinkle me with boiling oil, they have me devoured by dogs, they impale me alive on a stake,
and they cut off my head with a sword; yet those things do not exist in me,
nor am I seen to possess those qualities.’”
This too, monks, is a second way in which a wise person experiences happiness and joy in this very life.
Furthermore, monks, when a wise person has ascended to a seat or a couch,
or is lying on the ground, whatever wholesome deeds were previously performed by him— well-conducted actions of body and well-conducted actions of speech— [these come to mind].
At that time, his well-performed deeds of mind hang down upon him...
Just as, monks, the shadows of great mountain peaks hang down, hang down all around, and hang down completely over the earth in the evening,
even so, monks, when a wise person has mounted a chair, or mounted a bed, or is on the ground—
Whatever wholesome deeds he previously performed— well-conducted actions of body, well-conducted actions of speech,
and well-conducted actions of mind— at that time they hang over him, hang down toward him, and dangle before him.
In this regard, monks, it occurs to the wise person:
‘Indeed, no evil has been done by me, no cruelty, no wickedness;
what is beautiful has been done, what is wholesome has been done, a refuge for those who fear has been made.

To whatever destination belongs those who have not done evil, who have not done cruelty, who have not done wickedness, who have done what is beautiful, who have done what is wholesome, and who have made a refuge for those who fear—to that destination I go after passing away.’
Thus he does not grieve, does not weary, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion.
This too, monks, is the third kind of happiness and joy that a wise person experiences here and now in this very life.

Furthermore, monks, having practiced good conduct by body, having practiced good conduct by speech, and having practiced good conduct by mind, that wise person, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
“Monks, if one were speaking rightly,
it is of heaven alone that one could rightly say: ‘It is entirely desirable,
entirely lovely, entirely pleasing.’”
“Monks, it is not easy to find even a simile for how blissful the heavenly realms are.
When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One:
“But is it possible, Bhante, to provide a simile?”
“It is possible, monks,” the Blessed One said.
“Just as, monks, a wheel-turning monarch endowed with the seven treasures and four powers experiences happiness and joy on that account.
With which seven?”
In this case, monks, on the fifteenth day of the Uposatha, when a head-anointed Kṣatriya king has bathed his head, is observing the Uposatha,
and has ascended to the upper terrace of his excellent palace, the divine Wheel-Treasure appears before him— possessing a thousand spokes, with a rim, with a hub,
and complete in every respect.
Having seen this, it occurs to that consecrated kṣatriya king:

"I have indeed heard this: when, on the fifteenth day of the month, the Uposatha, a consecrated kṣatriya king has bathed his head, observed the Uposatha, and ascended to the upper terrace of his palace, the divine Wheel-Treasure appears to him."
‘With its thousand spokes, its rim, and its hub, complete in every respect—such is the Wheel-Turning Monarch.
‘Shall I indeed become a Wheel-Turning Monarch?
Then, monks, the anointed Kṣatriya king, taking the water-pitcher in his left hand, sprinkles the Wheel-Treasure with his right hand, saying:
"May your wheel-treasure turn, may your wheel-treasure conquer!
Then, monks, that wheel-treasure rolls toward the eastern direction, and the Wheel-turning Monarch follows right behind it with his fourfold army. And in whatever region, monks, the wheel-treasure...
The Wheel-Turning Monarch establishes himself there and takes up residence together with his fourfold army.
And those rival kings in the eastern direction, monks, approach the Wheel-Turning Monarch and say this:
“Come, Great King! Welcome to you, Great King! All is yours, Great King; please give us your command, Great King.”
The Wheel-turning Monarch speaks thus:
‘No living being is to be killed; what is not given is not to be taken; one must not engage in sexual misconduct; one must not speak falsehood; intoxicants are not to be drunk;
and you must eat only as much as is required. And those rival kings in the eastern direction, monks, become the vassals of that Wheel-turning Monarch.
Then, monks, that Wheel-Treasure, having plunged into the eastern ocean and emerged again, rolls toward the southern direction...
[as before] ...having plunged into the southern ocean and emerged again, it rolls toward the western direction...
[as before] ...having plunged into the western ocean and emerged again, it rolls toward the northern direction, following right after the king.
The wheel-turning monarch, together with his fourfold army. In whatever place, monks, the Wheel-Treasure halts, there the wheel-turning monarch takes up residence together with his fourfold army.
And those rival kings in the northern direction, monks, having approached the wheel-turning monarch, speak to him thus:
"Come, Great King! Welcome to you, Great King! Be seated, Great King! Command us, Great King! The Wheel-turning Monarch spoke thus:

"Living beings must not be killed; what is not given must not be taken; one must not engage in sexual misconduct; one must not speak falsehoods; intoxicants must not be drunk; and you must eat only as much as is required."
“Monks, as for the rival kings in the northern direction, they become subordinates to the Wheel-turning Monarch.
Then, monks, having conquered the earth bounded by the ocean,
that Wheel-treasure returns to that very royal capital and stands at the gate of the Wheel-turning Monarch’s inner palace as if fixed on its axle.”
Adorning the palace gate of the wheel-turning monarch.
Monks, such is the Wheel-Treasure that appears to the wheel-turning monarch.
Furthermore, monks, the Elephant-Treasure appears to the wheel-turning monarch—
There is a king of elephants named Uposatha, entirely white, with seven points of contact, possessed of supernormal power, and able to travel through the air.
Upon seeing him, the mind of the wheel-turning monarch becomes confident:
"How excellent indeed would be this elephant-vehicle, were it only to come under training!"
Then, monks, that elephant-treasure, just as a noble thoroughbred elephant well-trained for a long time would,
likewise submits to discipline. Once in the past, monks, the Wheel-turning Monarch, desiring to test that very elephant-treasure, mounted it in the morning,
traveled across the earth bounded by the ocean, and having returned to that very capital city, took his breakfast.
Monks, such is the elephant-treasure that appears for a wheel-turning monarch.
Furthermore, monks, the horse-treasure appears for a wheel-turning monarch:
entirely white, with a black head and a mane like muñja grass, possessed of supernormal power, able to travel through the air, the king of horses named Valāhaka.
Seeing this, the mind of the wheel-turning monarch becomes serene:
"How wonderful indeed, sir, is this horse-vehicle, were it only to come under training!
Then, monks, that jewel of a horse comes under training just as a noble thoroughbred horse, well-trained for a long time, would do.
In the past, monks, a wheel-turning monarch, desiring to test that very horse-treasure, would mount it in the morning,
travel across the earth as far as the ocean’s edge, and upon returning to that same royal capital, partake of his breakfast.
Such is the horse-treasure that appears to a wheel-turning monarch, monks.
Furthermore, monks, the jewel-treasure appears to the wheel-turning monarch.
It is a beryl gem, beautiful, of noble birth, eight-faceted, and well-polished.
And the radiance of that jewel-treasure, monks, pervades an area for a league all around.

In the past, monks, when a wheel-turning monarch was testing that very jewel-treasure, he would equip his fourfold army, hoist the jewel upon the top of his banner, and set out in the thick darkness of the night.
And those villages nearby, monks, by means of its radiance, would carry on their work, thinking, "It is day.
Such a jewel-treasure appears to a wheel-turning monarch, monks.
Furthermore, monks, the woman-treasure appears to the Wheel-turning Monarch.

She is beautiful, lovely, pleasing, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion; she is neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too stout, neither too dark nor too fair, surpassing human beauty yet not having reached divine beauty.
Moreover, monks, the touch of that woman-treasure’s body is like that of a tuft of cotton or a tuft of silk-cotton.
Moreover, monks, the limbs of that woman-treasure are warm in the cold and cool in the heat.
From her body, monks, the fragrance of sandalwood wafts forth, and from her mouth, the fragrance of blue lotuses wafts forth.
Furthermore, monks, that woman-treasure rises before the Wheel-turning Monarch and retires after him; she is attentive to his needs, acts agreeably, and speaks kindly.
Moreover, monks, that jewel of a woman does not transgress against the wheel-turning monarch even in thought, much less in body.
Such is the jewel of a woman that appears to the wheel-turning monarch.
Furthermore, monks, the jewel of a householder appears to the wheel-turning monarch.
The divine eye born of the ripening of his karma becomes manifest to him, by which he sees treasure—both that with an owner and that without an owner.
He approaches the Wheel-turning Monarch and says:
“Be at ease, Your Majesty; I shall perform for you whatever needs to be done with wealth.”

“Once upon a time, monks, a wheel-turning monarch, desiring to test that very treasure of the householder, boarded a boat, entered the current in the middle of the river Ganges, and said to the householder-treasure:
‘Householder, I have need of gold and bullion.
‘In that case, Great King, let the boat approach one bank,’ he replied.”
“‘Householder, my need for gold and bullion is right here!
Then, monks, that householder-treasure, dipping both hands into the water, drew up a jar full of gold and bullion and said this to the wheel-turning monarch:
‘That is enough, Great King! That much is sufficient, Great King! That much has been honored, Great King!’”
The wheel-turning monarch says this:
“Enough with that much, householder; it is done with that much, householder; it is honored with that much, householder.
Monks, such is the householder-treasure that appears to a wheel-turning monarch.
Furthermore, monks, the counselor-treasure appears to the Wheel-turning Monarch—
one who is wise, competent, intelligent, and capable of advising the Wheel-turning Monarch on whom he should approach, whom he should keep away from, and whom he should appoint.
He approaches the Wheel-turning Monarch and says this:
“Be free from anxiety, O King; I shall provide guidance.
Such is the counselor-treasure that appears to a Wheel-turning Monarch.
Monks, a Wheel-turning Monarch is endowed with these seven treasures.
By what four kinds of success?
Here, monks, a wheel-turning monarch is handsome, beautiful, pleasing, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion, far surpassing other men.
Monks, a wheel-turning monarch is endowed with this first kind of success.
Furthermore, monks, a wheel-turning monarch is long-lived and long-enduring, far exceeding other human beings.
Monks, a wheel-turning monarch is endowed with this second psychic power.

Furthermore, monks, a wheel-turning monarch is free from illness and free from affliction; he possesses a digestive system that is well-balanced, being neither too cold nor too hot, far exceeding that of other human beings.
Monks, a wheel-turning monarch is endowed with this third supernormal power.
Furthermore, monks, a wheel-turning monarch is dear and pleasing to the brahmins and householders,
just as a father is dear and pleasing to his children.
In the same way, monks, the wheel-turning monarch is dear and pleasing to the brahmins and householders.
And the brahmins and householders, monks, are dear and pleasing to the wheel-turning monarch.
Just as, monks, sons are dear and pleasing to a father;
In the same way, monks, the brahmins and householders are dear and pleasing to a wheel-turning monarch.
Once upon a time, monks, a wheel-turning monarch set out for a pleasure park with his fourfold army.
Then, monks, the brahmins and householders approached the wheel-turning monarch and said this:
“Drive slowly, Your Majesty, so that we may see you for a longer time.
Then, monks, the Wheel-turning Monarch addressed his charioteer:
“Drive slowly, charioteer, so that the brahmins and householders may see me for a longer time.”
Monks, a wheel-turning monarch is endowed with this fourth supernormal power.
Monks, a wheel-turning monarch is endowed with these four supernormal powers.
What do you think, monks?
“Would not a wheel-turning monarch, endowed with these seven treasures and these four supernormal powers, experience happiness and joy on that account?
“Venerable sir, a wheel-turning monarch would experience happiness and joy on account of even a single treasure, let alone on account of the seven treasures and the four supernormal powers.
Then the Blessed One took up a small stone the size of his hand and addressed the bhikkhus:
“What do you think, monks, which is greater:
this small pebble, the size of a hand, that I have taken up, or Himavā, the king of mountains?

“Venerable sir, the small pebble, the size of a hand, taken up by the Blessed One is insignificant; compared to Himavā, the king of mountains, it does not even bear mention, it does not bear comparison, it does not even admit of a fraction.”

“In the same way, monks, whatever happiness and joy a wheel-turning monarch experiences on account of being endowed with the seven treasures and the four powers does not approach even a fraction of divine happiness;
it does not approach a part of it, nor does it bear comparison to it.”
Monks, that wise person, if at some time or other, after the lapse of a long period, returns to the human state,
is reborn into a high-ranking family— either a wealthy kshatriya family, a wealthy brahmin family, or a wealthy householder family— one that is affluent,
possessing great wealth and vast resources, with abundant gold and silver, many possessions and implements, and ample riches and grain.

And he is handsome, pleasing, and attractive, endowed with supreme beauty of complexion; he is a recipient of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps.
He practices good conduct by body, good conduct by speech, and good conduct by mind.
Having practiced good conduct by body, good conduct by speech, and good conduct by mind, at the breaking up of the body after death, he reappears in a happy destination, a heavenly world.
“Monks, it is just as if a gambler were to win a great mass of wealth on his very first lucky throw.
That lucky throw by which the gambler wins a great mass of wealth on his very first throw, monks, is a minor stroke of luck. But this is a much greater stroke of luck than that:
namely, when a wise person, having practiced good conduct with the body, [wins the higher realms].”
Having practiced good conduct in speech and having practiced good conduct in mind, with the breakup of the body, after death,
one is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
This, monks, is the entire, complete ground of the wise.”
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
The bhikkhus were uplifted and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Ninth Discourse, "The Fool and the Wise," is concluded.
